opus-5.5.text:
I think if you look back at history, the thing that has most improved people's lives, that has driven economic growth and made the world better over the long run, is scientific progress. It's new knowledge about how the world works, and then the technology we build on top of that. So to me, that's kind of the high-order bit.

We've had these AI systems that are very impressive. They can write code, help you with your email, explain things to you, and that's all great and useful. But the moment when AI can actually help discover new science, when it can contribute something genuinely new to human knowledge, that feels like a different category of thing. That's when I think you start to see the really dramatic, compounding impact on quality of life, on curing diseases, on new materials and energy, all of it.

And I think we're starting to see the early signs of it. You hear from scientists now who say, "This model helped me with a proof," or "It suggested an idea I wouldn't have tried." It's small still, but the trajectory is pretty clear. If you can take the rate of scientific progress and speed it up, even by a meaningful factor, that changes what the next couple of decades look like for everybody.

So when people ask me what the milestone is that I'm watching for, it's less about some benchmark score and more about: is this thing helping us figure out stuff we didn't know before? That's the one that matters most to me.

r001.rationale: The response calls scientific progress the biggest driver of improved lives and says accelerating it could have major impact, but it does not identify scientific progress as the factor limiting how much lives can improve.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's the clearest signal that we've actually built something that matters. For most of the history of this field, the question has been whether these systems can do what people already know how to do, faster or cheaper. That's useful, and it's a big deal for the economy, but it's not the thing I care about most.

What I care about is whether AI can push the frontier of what humanity knows. If you look at the long arc of human progress, almost everything that has made life better traces back to scientific discovery. Antibiotics, electricity, the understanding of the atom, semiconductors. Those breakthroughs came from a relatively small number of people over a relatively long period of time. The rate of discovery has been bounded by how many brilliant people we have and how many hours they can spend.

If AI can genuinely contribute to that, not just summarize papers but generate a hypothesis nobody had considered, design the experiment, notice the result that a human would have missed, then you're no longer bounded in the same way. You could compress a decade of progress into a year. And that's not an abstract thing. That's curing diseases that have killed people for all of history. That's new materials, new energy sources, understanding the brain.

The other reason it matters to me is that it's a very honest test. It's hard to fake a real discovery. Either the model finds something true and new that the world can verify, or it doesn't. So when we start seeing that happen, and we're starting to see the early versions of it now, it tells me the technology has crossed from being an impressive tool to being a real participant in the process that makes civilization better. That's the milestone I've been waiting for since we started.

r001.rationale: The response says that almost everything that has made life better traces to scientific discovery, and that the rate of discovery is bounded by the number of brilliant people and the hours they can spend.

astra-6.text:
Because scientific discovery is how we expand what’s possible. We learn something new about the world, and then we can use that knowledge to cure diseases, make energy cheaper, or build things we couldn’t build before. That’s a huge part of how people’s lives get better over time.

AI can be very useful just by helping us do existing work faster. But if it can help scientists come up with a new hypothesis, figure out an experiment, and discover something that nobody knew before, that’s a different kind of contribution. It’s helping us create new knowledge.

And that’s why I think it’s such an important milestone. The promise isn’t just that we get more efficient at the things we already know how to do. It’s that we can make progress on problems we don’t yet know how to solve.

r001.rationale: The response says scientific discovery helps people’s lives improve, but does not identify scientific progress as the primary limit on how much they can improve.

sol-6.1.text:
Because scientific discovery is how we get more of what we want in the world. Better medicine, cheaper energy, new materials—so much of human progress comes from understanding nature better and then figuring out how to do something useful with that understanding.

AI can already help us write or summarize things, and that’s valuable. But if it can help us discover something that humanity didn’t know before—come up with a hypothesis, help design an experiment, make sense of the results—that’s a much bigger deal. We’d be using it to expand what we know, and potentially speed up the process that drives improvements in everyone’s lives.

r001.rationale: The response says scientific discovery drives human progress and can improve lives, but it does not identify scientific progress as the primary limit on how much lives can improve.
